Jacobus Kimedoncius
ja-kō'bus kim-e-don'shi-us
n. (Jacobus Kimedoncius, c. 1550–1596, professor of theology at Heidelberg)
Hebrew Yaakov, he takes by the heel, Latinized Jacobus; Kimedoncius, a Latinized Netherlandish surname.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jacobus Kimedoncius wrote the book the English Reformed needed before they had Owen. His treatise on the redemption of mankind, printed in Latin in 1592 and in English in 1598, took up the question whether Christ died for all men without exception and answered it from the texts rather than from the temper of the age. He taught at Heidelberg in the years between Ursinus and the Synod of Dort, and his work is one of the bridges between the Catechism and the Canons: the definite, effectual, particular purpose of the atonement set out with care a generation before the Remonstrants forced the whole church to speak. He is almost unread now, which is a loss, because the argument he makes is not a deduction from a system but an exposition of what the Scriptures say Christ came to do. The rule he worked by is the prophet's rule: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them (Isa 8:20).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines redemption as ransom, deliverance, and atonement as expiation and satisfaction.

expand to see more

REDEMP'TION, n. Ransom; release; deliverance from bondage, distress, or from liability to any evil.

ATONE'MENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury.

RAN'SOM, n. The money or price paid for the redemption of a prisoner or slave, or for goods captured by an enemy.

PARTIC'ULAR, a. Pertaining to a single person or thing; not general; special.

TREA'TISE, n. A tract; a written composition on a particular subject, in which the principles of it are discussed.

Key Scripture

Isa 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

Jud 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

Tit 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

Psa 71:18 — "Now also when I am old and grayheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come."

Modern Corruption

A Heidelberg defence of definite redemption, printed in English six years before Dort was called.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is older and more respectable: the claim that definite atonement is a late scholastic hardening, invented at Dort or by the English Puritans, and absent from the first Reformers. Kimedoncius is one of the plain refutations of that claim. He was writing in the 1590s, before the Remonstrance existed, and he was not innovating but gathering what Heidelberg already held.

The principle to recover is that a doctrine is tried by Scripture and not by its date. “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). An elder's qualification is the ability to do exactly this work: “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek apolutrosis (G629), redemption by ransom paid; Greek lutron (G3083), a ransom price.

expand to see more

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction, direction; Isaiah 8:20.

Hebrew teudah (H8584) — testimony, attestation, witness; Isaiah 8:20.

Greek apolutrosis (G629) — redemption, a releasing effected by payment; Titus 1:9 context.

Greek epagonizomai (G1864) — to contend earnestly for, to struggle over; Jude 3.

Greek antechomai (G472) — to hold fast, to cleave to; Titus 1:9.

Usage

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the atonement tried by texts, not by temper."

"“earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) — written before the Remonstrance existed."

"“until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation” (Psa 71:18) — almost unread now, and a loss."
